name: Arunajadeswarar Temple, Tiruppanandal
deity: Shiva as Arunajadeswarar (Thaalavaneswarar), with the goddess Periyanayaki
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Chola country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with Chola-era inscriptions and later additions
dynasty: Medieval Chola patrons and later rulers
summary: Arunajadeswarar is the Tevaram shrine of Thaalavaneswarar at Tiruppanandal, remembered for the leaning Shiva linga that bent to accept a devotee's garland and was set upright by the devotion of the saint Kungiliya Kalaya Nayanar.

sections.history: Tiruppanandal lies in the fertile Kaveri delta, in the Thiruvidaimarudur taluk of Thanjavur district, roughly midway between Kumbakonam and Gangaikonda Cholapuram. In the Tevaram the town is sung as Tiruppanandal, and the temple is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams on the northern bank of the Kaveri. Older names preserve its memory: Thadagaieswaram, for the devotee Thadagai, and Thala Vanam, the grove of palms from which the town takes its name. Inscriptions of the Chola kings are reported at the temple, and the shrine grew in stone under their patronage and that of later rulers. Within the complex stands the Kasi Mutt, the Saivite monastery founded by Kumaragurupara Desikar, which gives the town a living tradition of learning and service to this day.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered beneath a seven-tiered rajagopuram on the west, with a five-tiered gopuram on the east. Within, the sanctum of Arunajadeswarar holds the Shiva linga, and the goddess Periyanayaki, the great lady, is honoured in her own shrine. A palm, the sacred tree of the shrine, recalls the ancient palm grove, and a sacred spring, Nagakannika Theertham, is said to lie beneath the sixteen-pillared hall. Sculpture within the temple is said to recall the stories of Thadagai and of the saint who set the Lord upright. The name Arunajadeswarar means the Lord of the red matted locks, and the quiet stone corridors keep the dignity of an old sanctuary of the Chola country.
sections.legends: Tradition says the goddess Parvati performed penance in the grove of palms here, and that the Lord taught her in the form of the supreme teacher, which is why he is worshipped as Gnana Guru as well as Thaalavaneswarar, the Lord of the palm forest. The place's own great legend is that of Thadagai, a devoted woman who came each day to garland the Lord. One day, as she raised the garland, the upper end of her garment slipped. She could not hold the cloth and offer the garland at once, and the Lord, sparing her modesty, bent his head toward her and received the flowers. The linga has been remembered as leaning ever since. Later, when the temple was being restored, a Chola king, named in the sources as Manimudi Chola, tried to set the linga upright; elephants strained at ropes tied to it, but it would not move. Kungiliya Kalaya Nayanar, a devotee of Tirukkadaiyur who offered fragrant incense to Shiva, heard of this and hurried to the town. He tied a rope to the linga and the other end about his own neck, and pulled with the Panchakshara on his lips, ready to give his life. At that moment the Lord yielded and stood upright, and the king and his army saw what devotion had done where strength had failed. The tale is told in the Periya Puranam as one of the lives of the sixty-three Nayanmar saints.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the usual round of Shaiva worship: Maha Shivaratri, the monthly Pradosham, and the festivals of the Tamil months, with processions of the Lord and the goddess. Detailed festival dates for this temple were not available in the sources consulted, so confirm the calendar locally, as dates follow the Tamil lunar calendar.
sections.experience: Tiruppanandal suits a quiet, story-led visit. Enter beneath the gopuram and come first to the sanctum of Arunajadeswarar, then to the shrine of Periyanayaki. Take time to hear the story of Thadagai and of Kungiliya Kalaya Nayanar from the priests or the older devotees of the town; it is the key to the place, and it makes the stillness of the linga and the corridors speak. Devotees come in remembrance of the saint's courage and to ask for strength in trials. The Kasi Mutt within the temple complex adds to the sense of a living centre of Shaiva learning. The shrine of Tiruaappadi, a few kilometres away, rounds out a day among the Tevaram temples of the delta.

visit.timings: Commonly reported as open from early morning to noon and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruppanandal stands on the Kumbakonam–Anaikarai road, about 18 to 21 km from Kumbakonam (sources differ), which has the nearest major railway station. Tiruchirappalli, the nearest major airport, is roughly 100 km away (approximate). Regular buses serve the town, and the temple is in Tiruppanandal itself. The Tevaram shrine of Tiruaappadi is only about 2.5 km away, so the two can be visited together.
